passage:
Dear Swati,
Every morning on the bus, the same older boy gives me a thumbs-down and then a rude finger gesture when the teacher isn't looking. I know it's an insult. At first I wanted to do it back. Then I remembered what you said: don't feed it. So I stepped away, stayed calm and kept my face still. It still made my stomach hurt. Yesterday I told my class teacher, and they said thank you for telling them and that they would sort out the seating. I feel a little lighter. I'm not sure it will stop, but I'm glad I didn't answer with the same gesture and get in trouble too.
Neelam

qa.q: How often does the older boy give the thumbs-down?
qa.a: He does it every morning on the bus.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling as Neelam stayed calm and kept Neelam's face still?
qa.a: Neelam felt hurt and anxious, since it made the stomach hurt, but did not want to escalate. There is also relief at having told someone.

qa.q: What could Neelam do if it continues?
qa.a: Neelam can keep stepping away, tell the class teacher or another trusted adult again, and note what happened. Nobody has to handle it alone.

qa.q: How might the class teacher have seen Neelam's report?
qa.a: They thanked Neelam for telling them and promised to sort out the seating. They took it seriously as a safety concern and did not judge Neelam.

grounding: A teenager recognises thumbs-down and rude gestures as insults, steps back, stays calm and tells an adult.

passage: I'm Ramesh, and last term some older boys started giving me thumbs-down and a rude finger every time I walked past the ground. I wanted to shout back. Instead I did what my sports teacher once said: stop, breathe, walk away. It wasn't easy. My hands shook for a while. Yamini walked with me to the staff room, and I told the teacher exactly what happened and when. They listened, thanked me, and spoke to the boys. Was it fixed overnight? No. But I felt heard, and I didn't have to be cruel back. If you ever get the same, tell someone. You're not being a tattletale.

qa.q: Who walked with Ramesh to the staff room?
qa.a: Yamini walked with Ramesh.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when the hands shook after walking away?
qa.a: Ramesh was upset and probably scared and angry, but held back from hitting back. Feeling heard by the teacher helped afterwards.

qa.q: What could someone do if rude gestures keep coming from bullies?
qa.a: Step back, stay calm, tell a trusted adult exactly what happened and when, and go with a friend if that helps. Answering with insults could bring trouble.

qa.q: How might Yamini's company have helped Ramesh?
qa.a: Yamini stayed with Ramesh to the staff room, so Ramesh didn't face it alone. Having a friend nearby can make speaking up easier.

grounding: A teenager recognises rude gestures as insults from bullies, stays calm and tells a trusted adult.

passage:
Yesterday my brother Lalit had an argument over a cricket game with a boy from the next lane. As we walked home, the boy rode past on his bike and flashed the middle finger right at Lalit.
Lalit's jaw went tight, and his hands clenched. I thought he'd shout back. But he took a breath, stepped back onto the footpath, and kept walking with me.
"That boy did the same last week," he muttered.
When we got home, Lalit told Papa everything. Papa listened and said he'd speak to the boy's parents that evening, and that Lalit had done the right thing by staying calm.
I don't know if Lalit was angry or scared. Probably both.
- Lavanya

qa.q: What did the boy on the bike do?
qa.a: He flashed the middle finger right at Lalit.

qa.q: What might Lalit have been feeling when his hands clenched?
qa.a: Lalit was likely angry and possibly scared, but he chose to stay calm; Lavanya can't be sure which feeling was stronger.

qa.q: What did Lalit do that was safe and wise?
qa.a: He stepped back, stayed calm, and told Papa the same day, since it had happened before.

qa.q: How did Papa respond to Lalit?
qa.a: Papa listened, praised him for staying calm, and planned to speak to the boy's parents that evening.

grounding: An observer sees a teenager recognise a rude gesture as an insult, step back calmly, and tell an adult since it came from ongoing bullying.

passage:
Monday: In the class group chat, every message Mehak posted got a row of thumbs-down emojis from the same three girls. She stopped posting.
Wednesday: In the corridor, one of the girls flashed the middle finger at Mehak as she passed. Mehak's heart pounded. She didn't respond. She walked straight to the staffroom, took a breath, and knocked.
Sangeeta Ma'am, her class teacher, listened to everything, including the chat. "Thank you for telling me. This isn't okay, and it's not your fault."
That afternoon, Ma'am spoke with the three girls and called their parents.
Friday: The thumbs-downs stopped. Mehak posted in the group again, just a small message about homework.

qa.q: What did the three girls send in the group chat?
qa.a: A row of thumbs-down emojis.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when the girl flashed the middle finger?
qa.a: Mehak felt scared and upset, her heart pounding, but she stayed calm.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta Ma'am do that helped?
qa.a: She listened, told Mehak it wasn't her fault, spoke to the three girls, and called their parents that same afternoon.

qa.q: How might the three girls see their gestures after the teacher's talk?
qa.a: They might realise their gestures were bullying and could bring real consequences.

grounding: Over a week, a teenager faces thumbs-down and rude gestures as bullying, stays calm, tells a teacher, and the adult acts the same day.

passage:
"Lalremsiami, you want to know why I never make rude gestures, even in traffic? Let me, your Zeenat Aunty, tell you.
When I was fifteen, I was late for the school bus, and the driver drove off without me. I was so angry, I raised my middle finger at the bus as it left.
The next day, the driver told the principal. I was banned from the bus for a week. My father had to drive me every day, and I had to apologise to the driver in front of everyone.
I felt so ashamed. The driver hadn't done anything wrong. I'd just been late.
Rude gestures might feel good for a second, but they hurt people and they come back to you."

qa.q: How long was Zeenat banned from the bus?
qa.a: A week.

qa.q: What was young Zeenat feeling when she apologised to the driver?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, knowing the driver had done nothing wrong and she had been late.

qa.q: What choice inside the story led to the consequence?
qa.a: Zeenat's choice to raise her middle finger at the bus led to the ban and the public apology.

qa.q: How might the bus driver have felt seeing the gesture?
qa.a: The driver probably felt insulted and hurt, since he had only been doing his job.

grounding: An aunt recalls using a rude gesture as a teenager and the real consequences, showing such gestures hurt others.

passage: The inter-school football match in Darjeeling went ahead in a thin, cold drizzle, with their usual coach away at a wedding. Every time Dolma touched the ball, Pema from the other team jogged past and gave her a thumbs-down right in her face. By the second half it had become the raised middle finger, twice, and a muttered word Dolma wouldn't repeat. Her own hand twitched to give it straight back. She didn't. She stepped away, took a breath of the wet air, and jogged to the touchline, where Mr Lepcha, the substitute teacher, stood with an umbrella. "Sir, number 9 keeps making rude signs at me. It's been all match." Mr Lepcha thanked her, spoke to the referee at once, and Pema was cautioned. After the match he told the other school's teacher, and that evening he rang Dolma's mother.

qa.q: Why was the usual coach away?
qa.a: The coach was at a wedding.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when her hand twitched?
qa.a: She felt angry and insulted, tempted to give the gesture straight back, but chose to stay calm.

qa.q: Which steps did Dolma take, and how did Mr Lepcha respond?
qa.a: She stepped away, breathed and told Mr Lepcha, who spoke to the referee at once, told the other school's teacher and rang her mother that evening.

qa.q: What would change if Dolma had given the gesture back?
qa.a: Dolma could have been cautioned too, and the adults might have seen a two-way fight instead of one player being targeted.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager recognising repeated thumbs-down and rude gestures as targeted insults, staying calm, and telling an adult who acts the same day.
